risks.risk: Geological uncertainties and natural hazards at project sites
risks.note: Inaccessible terrain, logistics constraints and limits of investigation have serious consequences for execution; tunnelling under high superincumbent cover creates severe stress problems and heavy water ingress. Plants sit in mountainous, geologically active regions exposed to earthquakes, flash floods, landslides, avalanches, Landslide Lake Outburst Floods (LLOF) and Glacial Lake Outburst Floods (GLOF), which can damage infrastructure and cause severe operational disruption.

risks.risk: Time and cost overruns on hydro construction
risks.note: Hilly-terrain projects are exposed to landslides, hill-slope collapses, roadblocks, floods and cloud bursts that set back construction schedules; unpredictable geology in long tunnels such as the Head Race Tunnel, and the need to build road tunnels where rock is unstable, add cost. Law and order problems also cause overruns. Volatility in raw material prices and global supply-chain disruption for critical components such as transformers and solar modules are explicitly named as further cost-overrun drivers.

Projects require numerous statutory and non-statutory clearances from multiple agencies, organizations and states; the process is complex, tedious and time-consuming and sometimes leads to abnormal delay, affecting project implementation.

risks.risk: Difficulty securing long-term PPAs and PSAs for new capacity
risks.note: Beneficiaries prefer short-term purchases through power exchanges or e-procurement over long/medium-term PPAs, while hydro tariffs are relatively high because projects are site-specific with high initial investment. Excessive bidding in the RE sector over the past two years has produced a supply-demand mismatch; delayed connectivity availability and declining tariffs in successive bids make Power Sale Agreements hard to secure, so NHPC faces difficulty dispatching power from new projects under long-term PPAs.

risks.risk: High initial cost / high tariff and long gestation, with tariff subject to CERC regulation
risks.note: Hydro development involves long gestation and large initial investment, resulting in high initial tariff. Cash flow and revenue from operations vary with CERC tariff regulations notified from time to time. High initial cost and tariff can be detrimental to obtaining investment sanction and require extensive financial re-engineering and waivers from stakeholders.

risks.risk: Law & order and security threats; opposition to hydro projects
risks.note: Projects and power stations located near sensitive border areas and remote locations face law-and-order problems and officials posted there are prone to security threats. Separately, hydroelectric projects face opposition from certain pressure groups, which has created apprehension among developers as some projects get stalled.

risks.risk: Restrictive state hydro policies and dependence on few contractors
risks.note: Several state hydro policies require upfront premium and free power over and above mandated free power for project allocation, which CPSEs following Government of India norms find difficult to accept, hampering project acquisition. Separately, very few contractors in India can deliver in remote, difficult-access locations, increasing dependence on a limited contractor pool.

risks.risk: Climate change (BRSR material issue, rated Risk with negative financial implication)
risks.note: Extreme weather events - floods, reduced river flows - may disrupt operations and in extreme cases damage infrastructure, raising restoration costs. Mitigation cited: GLOF and LLOF studies and Early Warning Systems at all hydro projects in operation and under implementation established as an integrated hazard monitoring, forecasting and prediction system, plus emission reduction (e-vehicles, green hydrogen) and energy conservation measures.

risks.risk: Business concentration in a single activity and hydrology-dependent output
risks.note: 94.18% of turnover comes from power generation by hydro-electric power plants (wind 0.13%, solar 0.35%, trading 0.17%, consultancy 0.50%), and generation is subject to the inherent hydrology-related variability of river flows. [Provenance: the turnover-mix percentages appear in BRSR Section A items 16-17, which arrived in the SIBLING profile/governance/registry bundles; the routed risks_esg BRSR extract begins after that table. Included here because concentration is a structural risk even though the AR does not label it one.]

risks.risk: Other BRSR material issues rated as Risk: biodiversity conservation, safety & working conditions, and compliance
risks.note: Biodiversity - impacts of submergence areas require EIA-based, third-party-assessed project-specific Environmental Management Plans implemented with state government departments. Safety - construction and operation require strict safety adherence; failure impedes productivity and causes financial and reputational loss, mitigated through the Safety Policy, training, audits, monitoring and mock drills. Compliance - non-compliance can lead to legal penalties, operational disruption and reputational damage; all requisite statutory clearances are taken before construction starts and periodic compliance reports are filed. All three are rated as having negative financial implications.

themes.need: DISCOMs mandating firm/round-the-clock RE make BESS + pumped-hydro the bid differentiator, and in Q1FY27 storage demand ran ahead of supply. ADANIGREEN has 3.5 GWh of BESS installed (+1.9 GWh at Khavda this quarter), targets 10+ GWh this fiscal and 50 GWh by FY30 on a thumb-rule INR 25-30 lakh of EBITDA per MWh against ~INR 1.5cr/MWh of capex, and has contracted essentially all merchant/C&I capacity to sibling AESL on 25-year (solar/wind) and 15-year (battery) fixed-price PPAs targeting ~15-16% IRR - a pivot from merchant builder to fixed-return contracted IPP, with evacuation (not panels) named as the binding constraint. JSWENERGY added 873 MW in Q1 and ~1.1 GW since April - 36% of its 3 GW FY27 target already banked, Tidong Hydro commissioned four months early - and raised INR 10,150cr, taking net leverage 5.2x to 4.95x. On the equipment side SERVOTECH said its BESS pack capacity is fully booked ('we are not able to meet the demand') and committed to 2x capacity in 6 months, 3x by 21-Mar-2027 and 10x within 2 years. ACMESOLAR/KPIGREEN/SUZLON/INOXWIND attach storage to solar/wind; NTPC/NHPC/SJVN/TATAPOWER drive pumped-hydro and utility-scale storage.
themes.driver: BESS capacity commissioning against demand two independent managements (ADANIGREEN, SERVOTECH) say already exceeds supply; FDRE/peak-power tender awards; merchant DAM prices (JSWENERGY: INR 4.40 -> INR 5.10/unit, +16%) on +8.5% Q1 power demand.

business_model.body: NHPC generates and sells electricity, overwhelmingly from hydro-electric power stations (94.18% of turnover), with smaller solar, wind, power-trading and consultancy activities. Power is supplied to Distribution Companies (DISCOMs) including state electricity distribution companies, State Power Departments and private distribution companies. NHPC also renders consultancy in design and engineering, geotechnical investigations, construction, operations and maintenance and renovation/modernization of hydropower projects to public- and private-sector clients in domestic and international markets.

group_structure.title: Group structure (profile)
group_structure.body:
- NHDC Limited — subsidiary: 51.08% held by NHPC (AOC-1 Part A and BRSR Section A item 23). Shareholding pattern: NHPC 51.08%, Government of Madhya Pradesh 26%, Narmada Basin Projects Company Limited (wholly owned by GoMP) 22.92%. Operates Indira Sagar Power Station (1000 MW) and Omkareshwar Power Station (520 MW), plus the 8 MW Sanchi Solar Project and 88 MW Omkareshwar Floating Solar Project in Madhya Pradesh. Acquired 01-08-2000. [Activity description sourced from the Directors' Report text that arrived in the SIBLING strategy_outlook bundle, not in this bundle.]
- Chenab Valley Power Projects Limited (CVPPL) — subsidiary: 58.16% held by NHPC; JKSPDCL holds 41.84%. Incorporated June 2011, acquired 13-06-2011. Developing four hydro-electric projects in the UT of Jammu & Kashmir: Pakal Dul (1000 MW), Kiru (624 MW), Kwar (540 MW) and Kirthai-II (820 MW). Listed among subsidiaries yet to commence operations. [Project detail from the sibling strategy_outlook bundle.]
- Bundelkhand Saur Urja Limited (BSUL) — subsidiary: 90.63% held by NHPC; acquired 02-02-2015. Solar development arm (Kalpi 65 MW commissioned; implementing 1200 MW Solar Park at Jalaun and 45 MW at Madhogarh, UP).
- Jalpower Corporation Limited / Jal Power Corporation Limited — subsidiary: 100% held by NHPC; acquired 31-03-2021. Listed among subsidiaries yet to commence operations. The name is printed as 'Jalpower Corporation Limited' in Form AOC-1 and as 'Jal Power Corporation Limited' in BRSR Section A item 23; both spellings are reproduced as printed and not reconciled.
- Ratle Hydroelectric Power Corporation Ltd — subsidiary: 51.00% held by NHPC; acquired 01-06-2021. Listed among subsidiaries yet to commence operations.
- NHPC Renewable Energy Limited (NHPC REL) — subsidiary: 100% held by NHPC; acquired 16-02-2022. Specialized renewable-energy arm (0.7 MW solar plant at Central University Ajmer).
- Loktak Downstream Hydroelectric Corporation Limited (LDHCL) — subsidiary: 74% held by NHPC; Government of Manipur holds 26%. Acquired 23-10-2009; incorporated October 2009 to execute the Loktak Downstream Hydro-electric Project (66 MW) in Noney District, Manipur. Yet to commence operations; the process of initiation of closure of LDHCL is under progress subject to approval of DIPAM, Ministry of Power and Govt. of Manipur. [Closure status from the sibling strategy_outlook bundle.]
- National High Power Test Laboratory Private Limited (NHPTL) — associate: 12.50% held by NHPC; associated 22-05-2009. Incorporated May 2009 to set up an online high power test laboratory for short-circuit testing; has set up a laboratory for testing 400 kV and 765 kV High Voltage Transformers at Bina, Madhya Pradesh, already operational. Principal place of operation India. Latest audited balance sheet date 31st March 2025; management-certified accounts were used for group consolidation for FY ended 31.03.2026.
- APGENCO NHPC Green Energy Limited (ANGEL) — JV: 50% held by NHPC (APGENCO holds the other 50%); associated 23-01-2025. demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- India's commitment to 500 GW of non-fossil fuel capacity by 2030 and Net-Zero emissions by 2070 places renewable and hydro power at the centre of the country's energy strategy
- Rising electricity demand driven by industrialisation, electrification of mobility and data-centre growth
- Hydropower is being recognised afresh for grid balancing, peaking support and round-the-clock storage through pumped storage projects
- Government initiatives creating a conducive environment for capacity addition: Hydro Purchase Obligation, tariff rationalisation for legacy projects, budgetary support for enabling infrastructure in Himalayan and North-Eastern States, and renewed thrust on PSPs
- Generation is subject to inherent hydrology-related variability of river flows; operations focus on plant availability, efficient reservoir management and preventive maintenance
- For new project financing, CERC Regulations govern the debt-equity structure; NHPC states it has sufficient internal resources for the equity component of future capex targets
- Credit standing as a driver of funding cost and access: highest domestic rating 'AAA' (stable) from ICRA, CARE and India Ratings, and international rating 'Baa3' (stable) from Moody's, at par with sovereign
- Consolidated installed capacity, together with subsidiaries and joint ventures, crossed 9333 MW from 31 power stations, with a further 17 projects aggregating 9204 MW under construction
- CVPPL (58.16% NHPC / 41.84% JKSPDCL) is developing four hydro-electric projects in the UT of Jammu & Kashmir: Pakal Dul HE Project (1000 MW), Kiru HE Project (624 MW), Kwar HE Project (540 MW) and Kirthai-II HE Project (820 MW)
- ANGEL (50:50 NHPC-APGENCO JV) is pursuing three projects aggregating 3270 MW: Gadikota (1200 MW), Aravetipalli (1320 MW) and Deenepalli (750 MW)
- Nepal: NHPC is associated with three hydropower projects - West Seti (800 MW), Seti River-6 (460 MW) and Phukot Karnali (624 MW); DPRs for West Seti and Seti River-6 submitted to Investment Board Nepal, technical clearance to the Final DPR of West Seti accorded by IBN in August 2025; Inception Report and DPR Review Report for Phukot Karnali submitted to VUCL, Nepal

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: NHPC is executing a large multi-technology expansion programme. On hydro, the group had 17 projects aggregating 9204 MW under construction and added a record 1850 MW in FY 2025-26 (Subansiri Lower 750 MW, Parbati-II 800 MW, Karnisar Solar 300 MW). On renewables, commissioned RE plants (including subsidiary companies) total 565.78 MW - 50 MW wind at Jaisalmer, 50 MW solar at Theni & Dindigul, the 300 MW Karnisar solar plant at Bikaner (COD of full capacity declared w.e.f. October 16, 2025), 0.7 MW at Central University Ajmer via NHPC REL, 65 MW at Kalpi via BSUL, 88 MW Omkareshwar floating solar and 8 MW Sanchi solar via NHDC, and 4.08 MW rooftop solar. As a developer NHPC is implementing 1197.68 MW of RE projects on EPC mode: 600 MW Kutch (Gujarat) and 100 MW N.P. Kunta (Andhra Pradesh) under the CPSU Scheme, 200 MW each at GSECL Solar Park Khavda Stage-1 and Stage-3 (Gujarat) under TBCB, 50 MW floating solar at West Kallada (Kerala), 40 MW at Ganjam (Odisha) and 7.68 MW rooftop under PM Surya Ghar. Stated timelines: N.P. Kunta targeted for Q2 FY 2026-27 and Kutch for Q4 FY 2026-27; both Khavda TBCB projects anticipated in Q2 FY 2026-27 subject to transmission connectivity; West Kallada and Ganjam targeted during FY 2026-27. Beyond its own balance sheet, NHPC acts as a Renewable Energy Implementing Agency (REIA) with 6278 MW under construction (649 MW Phase-I, 5129 MW under the MNRE FY2023-24 bidding calendar, 500 MW FDRE under FY2024-25) and 1570 MW already commissioned through developers in Rajasthan; a further 12832 MW awaits PSA/PPA signing (1812 MW from FY2023-24 and 11020 MW from FY2024-25). Under Phase-I NHPC awarded 2000 MW of solar of which 1351 MW is commissioned/partially commissioned, 349 MW is expected in FY 2026-27 and 300 MW is held up on GIB and connectivity issues (sub-judice before CERC). As a BESS Implementing Agency, NHPC has awarded the entire 1500 MWh allocated under the VGF scheme - 500 MWh in Kerala at 4 locations (single-cycle 4-hour) and 1000 MWh in Andhra Pradesh at 3 locations (two-cycle 2-hour) - all expected to be commissioned during FY 2026-27. Subsidiary BSUL is implementing a 1200 MW Solar Park at Jalaun, Uttar Pradesh and a 45 MW solar project at Madhogarh; 95.26 MW of rooftop solar is in various stages (2.78 MW own stations/offices, 67.53 MW allocated States/UTs, 24.95 MW Central Ministries) with five States/UTs (Haryana, J&K, Sikkim, Manipur, Nagaland) and eight Central Ministries assigned under PM Surya Ghar. A 25 kWe pilot Green Hydrogen project at Leh and a pilot green hydrogen-based e-mobility project at Chamba (Himachal Pradesh) are in advanced stages of implementation. BRSR-stated capacity goals: install 3,000 MW hydro and 1,200 MW other renewable capacity by 2030, achieve 38,500 MW by FY 2033-34 and become a 50,000 MW company by 2047; against these, 9,454 MW across 16 RE projects (10 hydro, 6 solar) is reported under construction.

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- Established track record in developing hydroelectric projects across the country with a competent, experienced workforce skilled in conceptualization, construction, commissioning and operation of hydro projects
- Full capability from concept to commissioning including a full-fledged in-house Design division, giving an edge over other hydro power companies in complex Himalayan environments

- Full-fledged in-house Survey Group with a centralized survey data bank, reducing dependency on outside agencies and saving cost and time
- Extensive experience constructing and operating hydroelectric projects in complex geological regions - remote hilly areas with inaccessibility, poor logistics, adverse climate and complex rock conditions; erection protocols standardized to international standards

risks.title: Risks & watch-items
risks.body:
- **Regulatory/tariff risk:** entire earnings reset hinges on CERC accepting high Subansiri (₹7.50/unit) and Parbati-II revised costs; any disallowance hits returns. Mgmt confident but it is the central swing factor.
- **Geological/execution risk:** Teesta-VI HRT geological issue slowing progress; hydro inherently surprise-prone (mgmt acknowledges "can never avoid a surprise").
- **RE offtake risk:** discoms hesitant to sign standalone-solar PPAs (connectivity only by 2029–30; demand for RTC/solar+wind+battery) — 14,000 MW of bid-out RE remains without PPA.
- **PAF dip:** 9M PAF 79.27%, ~3% below prior-year due to monsoon shutdowns (Dulhasti, Salal, Chamera-I/III).
- **Other-income decline** (lower insurance/business-interruption realisations) is a real headwind to reported numbers.

non_obvious.title: Non-obvious takeaways
non_obvious.body:
- **Reported PAT understates run-rate:** 80%-revenue booking + 100% expense recognition on Parbati-II/Subansiri means the earnings inflection is back-loaded to CERC final orders (5–6 months for Parbati-II) — a potential re-rating catalyst rather than current-quarter event.
- **PSP is the strategic pivot:** management explicitly frames PSP/storage as the monetisation of grid solar build-out ("we definitely require storage… 100% sure we can sell").
- **Etalin shifting onto NHPC's balance sheet** materially enlarges the long-term hydro asset base (3,097 MW, India's largest hydro project) — capex commitment but regulated-asset growth.
- **RE PPA bottleneck is sector-wide** (connectivity 2029–30, discoms wanting RTC), not NHPC-specific — affects all REIAs.
